item.title: Anthropic mathematician claims independent Riemann Hypothesis proof using Claude
item.description:
Anthropic mathematician claims independent Riemann Hypothesis proof using Claude

Within a few hours of each other, two mathematicians claimed independent proofs of the Riemann Hypothesis, the most famous open problem in mathematics. Levent Alpöge of Anthropic first made his Claude-driven proof in a note released with Lean code rather than a full paper, while Alessandro Masullo released his 940-page, 100% human work-in-progress proof.

🧩 How it works

Levent Alpöge states that he is presenting the world with a complete argument before having mastered a massive neighbourhood around its mathematics. To avoid posting an unreadable travesty of “slop”, he decided to only present the Lean code. The artifact consists solely of Lean code, which is 1.3GB worth and equivalent to approximately 250,000 pages if written out in prose.

The work began on October 6. Eight of the 20 steps landed on November 15, and the final entry on November 16 reads “GRH.” Alpöge credits Claude for the parts involving automorphic forms on higher-rank groups, an area where he says he has little mastery. As Alpöge noted, “Claude far outpaced me near the finish line. No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.”

⚙️ Key details

  • Formalized Statement: Elliot Glazer confirms that the formalized statement is the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH).
  • Verification: Glazer puts the chance of a Lean bug at well under 1%. If the code finishes compiling with no extra axioms, it is probably correct, even though no human will ever have read all of it.
  • Human Alternative: Alessandro Masullo’s proof is a roughly 940-page GRH draft. It is reported as 100% human and had been undergoing secret manual review and revision per Kevin Hartnett for the last 12 years.
  • Uncertainties: The specific Claude model used and the degree of human steering have not been disclosed.
  • Market Reaction: ANT stock fell about 10% on the day of the announcement.

💡 Why it matters

This development is the third in a trilogy of frontier math breakthroughs, following the Navier Stokes solutions and the Quasi-Riemann bounding. However, both AI-claimed Millennium Prize results will take years to verify.

OpenAI’s September Navier-Stokes claim remains a cautionary tale, as critics argued that its Lean proof did not match the natural-language result. Artificial Analysis notes that this Riemann Hypothesis claim and the previous Navier-Stokes claim are currently unverified.

The situation highlights a distinct contrast: the AI-written solution is probably correct but incomprehensible, while the human solution is probably technically incorrect but understandable. This underscores the need for Weak to Strong alignment in the open-ended domain of controlling AI that is smarter than humans, raising questions about the No Slop Manifesto tenet that one should understand what they ship.

#RiemannHypothesis #Anthropic #FormalVerification #LeanCode #AIResearch

Source: Riemann Hypothesis proved…twice independently — Latent Space

item.title: NVIDIA Dynamo Optimizes RL Training via Routing and Weight Updates
item.description:
NVIDIA Dynamo Optimizes RL Training via Routing and Weight Updates

NVIDIA has introduced Dynamo as a serving layer designed to address constraints in reinforcement learning (RL) training, helping teams generate more accepted training samples and complete training iterations faster. By addressing bottlenecks in rollouts, weight updates, and worker recovery, the framework aims to prevent GPU capacity waste and training delays as RL workloads scale.

🧩 How RL Training Scales

Reinforcement learning uses rewards to train models to solve problems and complete tasks. The training process relies on several key components:

  • Workers generate rollouts, which are sequences of model outputs, actions, and environment interactions.
  • RL Frameworks score the results, update model weights, and send those weights back to the workers for the next round.
  • Dynamo sits between rollout orchestration and inference workers, routing generation requests from the RL framework to eligible inference capacity.

⚙️ Key Details: Addressing Training Bottlenecks

As RL training scales, redundant compute, slow rollouts, and worker failures can delay progress. Dynamo addresses these issues through specific mechanisms:

  • Routing and Cache Reuse: Multiple RL attempts often begin with identical instructions or contexts. Dynamo’s router balances KV cache reuse and worker load, sending requests to workers that have already cached the prompt to avoid repeated processing.
  • ModelExpress Weight Updates: Sending full model checkpoints to every worker is time-consuming and can interrupt generation. ModelExpress uses delta weight transfer, sending a compressed representation of what changed rather than the full model. Compatible workers can also copy weights directly from another GPU over NIXL.
  • Recovery and Resilience: When a worker fails, Dynamo detects the loss and directs new requests toward eligible healthy workers. It adds replacement workers to the routing pool once they have loaded a checkpoint and applied subsequent deltas to catch up.

📊 Real-World Applications

Several organizations have utilized NVIDIA Dynamo and ModelExpress to optimize their RL workloads:

Organization Application
Microsoft AI Used Dynamo to support RL rollout inference during post-training.
CoreWeave Uses Dynamo and ModelExpress to accelerate model weight updates by up to 15×.
Cognition Used Dynamo to manage inference workers and route rollouts during the post-training of SWE-1.7.
Prime Intellect Uses Dynamo for distributed inference orchestration.
H Company Used Dynamo and ModelExpress to reduce average training-step time by up to 20% and GPU-hours by up to 5%.

💡 Why it matters

Addressing rollout bottlenecks allows teams to complete more training iterations within a fixed compute budget. By ensuring that GPU capacity is not wasted on redundant prefix processing or slow weight transfers, Dynamo helps maintain the momentum of the training run, even as model weights are updated and infrastructure fails.

#NVIDIA #ReinforcementLearning #Dynamo #GPUTechnology #LLMTraining

Source: Reducing Rollout Bottlenecks in Reinforcement Learning with NVIDIA Dynamo | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: Bi-directional KV Cache Transfer Cuts Latency for Multi-turn AI Agents
item.description:
Bi-directional KV Cache Transfer Cuts Latency for Multi-turn AI Agents

Multi‑turn agentic workloads accumulate context as an agent reasons, invokes tools, and incorporates earlier results. Each new turn resends the full conversation history – system instructions, prior prompts, tool results, and model responses – causing the growing context to be processed repeatedly.

🔍 Overview

  • In Prefill‑decode (P‑D) disaggregation, a prefill node builds the key‑value (KV) cache for the prompt, while a decode node retrieves those KV blocks to generate the response.
  • Conventional disaggregated serving moves KV cache only from prefill → decode. This one‑directional flow creates two inefficiencies for multi‑turn workloads:
    1. After a response, the decode node holds KV entries for both the prompt and newly generated tokens. The prefill node cannot retrieve these entries for the next turn and must recompute KV projections for the previous response tokens.
    2. Session state is kept on the decode node but not on prefill nodes, increasing the chance of cache eviction for active sessions on the prefill side.
  • When a full cache miss occurs, the prefill node recomputes KV projections for the entire conversation history, consuming more accelerator capacity and increasing time‑to‑first‑token (TTFT).

#AIInference #KVCache #MultiTurnAgents #AWS

Source: Improve TTFT for multi-turn agentic workloads with bi-directional KV transfer in vLLM | Amazon Web Services
